mean: worried and a little scared about something that is about to happen
ex: Kavya was so nervous before her first board exam that she checked her admit card five times.
ex2: Abdul was nervous about asking his boss for a raise, so he practised his lines in the lift.
note: Nervous is about something coming soon and usually passes; anxious is deeper worry that can last much longer.

mean: happy because a worry or problem has gone away
ex: Mrs Fernandes was relieved when the doctor said her son only had a mild viral fever.
ex2: Fans at Eden Gardens were relieved when the rain stopped and the umpires said the match would go on.
note: Say 'relieved to hear/know' + the news. The noun is 'relief', as in 'What a relief!'

mean: sad because you are alone or have no one close to you
ex: In his first month at the Pune hostel, Arjun felt lonely until he joined the college quiz club.
ex2: After her children moved abroad, Mrs Kulkarni felt lonely in the big Nagpur flat until she joined a morning laughter club.
note: Alone is a fact (no one is with you); lonely is a feeling. You can be alone and happy, or lonely in a crowd.

mean: feeling thankful for something someone did for you
ex: Ramesh, a farmer in Vidarbha, was grateful to the neighbours who lent him their tractor during sowing.
ex2: Neha was grateful to the stranger on the Delhi metro who ran after her to return the wallet she had dropped.
note: Grateful TO a person, FOR a thing. Spelling trap: it is 'grate-ful', not 'great-ful'.

mean: feeling silly and awkward because others saw a small mistake
ex: Siddharth was embarrassed when he slipped on the wet platform in front of a packed Mumbai local.
ex2: Rakesh was embarrassed when his mother showed his baby photos to all the guests at his engagement.
note: Embarrassed = awkward about a harmless, public slip; ashamed = guilty about something truly wrong. Spell it with double r and double s.

mean: worried and uneasy, often for a long time, about what might happen
ex: Priya's parents grew anxious when her flight from Chennai was delayed and her phone stayed switched off.
ex2: Farmers in Punjab are anxious about the late monsoon, because their paddy needs water right now.
note: 'Anxious to do something' can also mean eager: 'She is anxious to start her new job.' Say ANGK-shus, not 'ang-zee-us'.

mean: upset because you keep trying but cannot do or change something
ex: Imran grew frustrated when the passport website crashed for the fifth time before he could pay.
ex2: The fans grew frustrated as their striker missed three easy chances in the Santosh Trophy final.
note: Frustrated is about blocked effort; exasperated is patience worn out by someone or something that keeps going wrong.

mean: wanting something good that another person has
ex: Tanvi was a little envious of her cousin's job in Bengaluru, though she was genuinely happy for her.
ex2: Stuck for two hours in Gurugram traffic, Kiran was envious of colleagues who could work from home.
note: Envious: you want what someone else has. Jealous: you fear losing what is yours. Indians often say 'jealous' for both; careful speakers don't.

mean: afraid someone will take away a person or thing you love
ex: Little Aarav got jealous when his grandmother spent the whole Diwali evening playing with the new baby.
ex2: Varun gets jealous whenever his girlfriend laughs with her old college friend at parties.
instead: upset someone else gets the attention
note: Strictly, jealous = guarding what is yours (love, attention); envious = wanting what is theirs. In casual talk, jealous is used for both.

mean: feeling there is too much at once: work, emotion or news
ex: With three deadlines and her sister's wedding in the same week, Meenal felt completely overwhelmed.
ex2: The small village clinic was overwhelmed when fifty people came in with fever after the floods.
note: It can be good too: 'overwhelmed by everyone's love' at a farewell. Say 'overwhelmed by/with', not 'overwhelmed from'.

mean: fondly missing a happy time from your past
ex: The smell of first rain on the school ground made Joseph nostalgic for his childhood in Kottayam.
ex2: The old Doordarshan theme music always makes my father nostalgic for Sunday mornings in the eighties.
note: Nostalgic looks back at the past with sweet sadness; wistful longs for something you cannot have, past or not.

mean: feeling bad about yourself because you did something wrong
ex: Rohit felt ashamed that he had shouted at the old chaiwala over two rupees of change.
ex2: Priya was ashamed of lying to her best friend about why she had skipped her birthday party.
note: Ashamed = guilt about doing wrong; embarrassed = awkward about a harmless slip. You are embarrassed by a torn kurta, ashamed of a lie.

mean: a little worried that something bad or difficult may happen
ex: Gurpreet was apprehensive about moving to Chennai, since she did not speak a word of Tamil.
ex2: Many shopkeepers in the old market were apprehensive about the new parking rules, fearing customers would stop coming.
note: Calmer and more formal than 'scared', and always about the future. Don't mix it up with 'comprehensive'.

mean: angry for a long time because you feel you were treated unfairly
ex: Suresh remained resentful for years that his younger brother was given the family shop in Indore.
ex2: The junior staff grew resentful when only the manager got credit for a project they had all worked on.
note: Resentment is old, quiet anger that keeps coming back, not a quick flash of temper. Naming it is the first step to letting it go.

mean: quietly happy and satisfied with what you have
ex: Lakshmi Amma is content with her small garden, her old radio and her evening filter coffee.
ex2: After years of rushing around Mumbai, Rafiq is content running a small bakery in his hometown, Bhopal.
note: As this adjective, stress the second part: kun-TENT. The noun 'content' (YouTube content, table of contents) is KON-tent.

mean: having mixed feelings, partly for something and partly against it
ex: Fatima felt ambivalent about the transfer to Dubai: more money, but far from her ageing parents.
ex2: Many residents felt ambivalent about the new flyover: traffic would move faster, but the old banyan trees had to go.
note: Ambivalent is not 'indifferent'. Ambivalent means you care in two directions at once; indifferent means you don't care.

mean: extremely happy and excited because of good news
ex: The whole village was elated when Kiran from the government school cleared the IIT entrance exam.
ex2: Divya was elated when her first painting sold on the opening day of the Kala Ghoda festival.
note: Elated is the high you feel right after good news. More formal than 'over the moon'.

mean: angry because something is unfair or wrong
ex: Passengers were indignant when the airline cancelled the flight and then refused to give refunds.
ex2: Old Mr Sethi was indignant when a young man pushed ahead of him in the queue at the ration shop.
note: Indignant anger is about injustice, often done to others. 'Righteous indignation' is a common phrase.

mean: very annoyed because something keeps going wrong or someone won't listen
ex: Exasperated after calling them ten times, Mrs Banerjee switched off the Wi-Fi to get the kids to dinner.
ex2: The exasperated maths teacher wrote the same sum on the board for the third time.
note: Exasperated = patience used up by repeated trouble; frustrated = blocked from reaching a goal.

mean: gently sad while longing for something you cannot have
ex: Dadi gave a wistful smile as she turned the pages of old photos of her childhood home in Lahore.
ex2: Watching students laugh in the college canteen, Professor Rao felt wistful about his own hostel days.
note: Wistful is soft and quiet, not deep grief. It often describes a smile, a look or a tone of voice.

mean: a deep, quiet sadness that stays for a while
ex: There is a gentle melancholy in the old Hindi film songs that Anwar plays on rainy evenings.
ex2: A quiet melancholy filled the empty hostel corridors on the last day of term.
note: Also an adjective ('a melancholy tune'). A literary word for a mood, music or place, not a medical term. Stress the first syllable.

mean: proved right after others doubted or blamed you
ex: When his food startup finally made a profit, Harsh felt vindicated; his relatives had called it a waste of money.
ex2: The umpire felt vindicated when the TV replay showed the batsman had clearly edged the ball.
note: Use it only when you were doubted or blamed first. The verb is 'vindicate': 'The report vindicated the nurses.'

mean: disappointed after learning something is not as good as you believed
ex: After two years of unpaid assistant jobs, Ankit grew disillusioned with the film industry.
ex2: Many young engineers grow disillusioned when their dream job turns out to be fixing spreadsheets all day.
note: It means your illusions were broken, not that you have them. Say 'disillusioned with', not 'disillusioned from'.

mean: extremely happy and excited, often together with a crowd
ex: Euphoric fans danced on Marine Drive late into the night after India won the World Cup.
ex2: Shruti was euphoric after finishing her first full marathon in Hyderabad, even though her legs could barely move.
note: Stronger than elated, and usually short-lived. The noun is 'euphoria': 'the euphoria after the result'.

mean: a secret pleasure at someone else's trouble or failure
ex: When the rude neighbour's shiny car splashed into a pothole, Rahul felt a small flash of schadenfreude.
ex2: There was a little schadenfreude in the office when the boss who banned tea breaks spilled chai on his own laptop.
instead: secret joy at their bad luck
note: A German word (harm + joy) with no neat English or Hindi equal. People usually admit to it with a little guilt.

mean: sad, alone and without hope; looking left behind
ex: A forlorn puppy sat outside the closed chai stall in the rain until Sana carried it home.
ex2: A forlorn old man sat alone on the station bench long after the last train to Siliguri had left.
note: Often describes how someone or something looks. 'A forlorn hope' is a plan that is very unlikely to work.

mean: unhappy and worried because something bad has happened
ex: Chhotu was upset when his kite got stuck on the neighbour's roof on Makar Sankranti.
ex2: Mrs Das was upset that nobody in the family group replied to her birthday wishes.
note: Say 'upset about something' and 'upset with someone'. An 'upset stomach' means a stomach that is unwell.

mean: pleased about something good you or someone close to you did
ex: Balwinder Singh was so proud when his daughter marched in the Republic Day parade in Delhi.
ex2: Aisha felt proud of herself for finishing a whole Tamil novel without a dictionary.
note: 'Proud of' someone is warm; but a 'proud' person can also mean an arrogant one, so watch the context.

mean: tired and restless because nothing interesting is happening
ex: Stuck at home during the long power cut, the kids were bored by noon.
ex2: Raghav got bored in the four-hour wedding ceremony and started counting the marigolds on the mandap.
note: 'I am bored' = I feel it. 'I am boring' = other people find me dull. A very common mix-up.

mean: feeling bad because you know you did something wrong
ex: Ankita felt guilty for eating the last gulab jamun that her brother had saved for after dinner.
ex2: Working late every night, Dev felt guilty about missing his son's school sports day.
note: Guilty is about the wrong you did; ashamed is about what you are, or how others would see you.

mean: sad because you are far from your home and family
ex: In her first winter in Delhi, Lalremruati felt homesick for Aizawl and her mother's cooking.
ex2: The young jawan posted in Ladakh felt homesick when he heard Lohri songs on the radio.
note: Homesick is about a place you are away from; nostalgic is about a time that has passed.

mean: not confident about yourself or your place among others
ex: Kunal felt insecure in the new class because everyone else spoke fluent English.
ex2: The senior bowler grew insecure when the selectors picked a faster youngster for the Ranji squad.
note: It can also mean 'not safe', as in an insecure job or an insecure password.

mean: unable to stay calm or still, from worry or boredom
ex: Waiting for her board results, Simran was so restless that she cleaned the whole cupboard twice.
ex2: After ten years at the same bank desk, Thomas felt restless and began looking at jobs in the Gulf.

mean: sad and without hope after something has gone wrong
ex: The dejected team sat silently in the dressing room after losing the final by one run.
ex2: Ajay looked dejected when the bank turned down his loan for the second time.
note: Dejected usually follows a defeat or a rejection; it is a low feeling, but often passes.

mean: made to feel foolish and small in front of others
ex: Sameer felt humiliated when the teacher read out his low marks to the whole class.
ex2: The old shopkeeper felt humiliated when a customer shouted at him in front of his own son.
note: Stronger than embarrassed: embarrassed is awkward, but humiliated hurts your self-respect.

mean: a little awkward because you did something silly or wrong
ex: Vikram gave a sheepish grin when his mother found the broken vase behind the sofa.
ex2: Arriving an hour late for the online interview, Nisha gave a sheepish apology.
note: Used for the look on your face after a small mistake, not for serious shame.

mean: nervous and confused, especially when rushed
ex: The new waiter at the Udupi restaurant got flustered when a table of twelve all ordered at once.
ex2: Asked a surprise question at the viva, Gaurav got flustered and forgot the formula he knew well.

mean: very sad and having lost hope
ex: After the hailstorm flattened his wheat, the farmer was despondent for weeks.
ex2: Her friends took a despondent Kavita out for chaat after she failed her driving test a third time.
note: Stronger and longer-lasting than dejected.

mean: tired and bored after having too much of something
ex: After twenty years of covering elections, the reporter was so jaded that nothing surprised him.
ex2: Even jaded Mumbaikars stopped to watch the first monsoon waves crash over the Worli sea face.

mean: sorry and feeling bad about something wrong you did
ex: A contrite Bilal returned the borrowed scooter with a full tank and a box of sweets.
ex2: The delivery app sounded contrite in its apology after customers' addresses were leaked.
note: Formal. Close to remorseful; contrite often shows in how you behave afterwards.

mean: a dull, empty feeling of being bored with everything
ex: During the long summer break, a heavy ennui settled over the empty hostel, and even card games felt pointless.
ex2: To escape the ennui of desk work, Rashid started weekend treks in the Western Ghats.
note: A French word, said on-WEE. Deeper than plain boredom: you are bored with life, not just with a film.

mean: annoyance and disappointment, often because you look foolish
ex: To Sunita's chagrin, the guests arrived just as the power went out and the dal got burnt.
ex2: Much to the captain's chagrin, the easy catch he dropped cost his team the match.
note: Almost always used as 'to someone's chagrin'. British say SHAG-rin; Americans say shuh-GRIN.
